title: Registers, commonplace books and the nineteenth-century reader
bodyMd:
Historians reconstructing what ordinary nineteenth-century readers actually read have long relied on library borrowing registers, which record each loan by title and by borrower. The registers are seductive because they are quantitative: they can be counted, tabulated and compared across towns. Yet a register records a transaction, not an encounter. A volume borrowed and returned unopened leaves precisely the same trace as one read aloud nightly to a family of eight. Ahlgren has argued that a neglected source — the commonplace book, the personal notebook in which a reader copied out passages that struck her — records the encounter rather than the transaction, and that the two sources, read together, can distinguish what circulated from what was absorbed.

The objection to Ahlgren's proposal is one of sampling. Commonplace books survive in numbers far smaller than registers, and they survive unevenly: the practice of keeping one was taught in schools that served a narrow band of the population, and the notebooks that reached archives are overwhelmingly those of families prosperous enough to keep papers for a century. A corpus so selected, critics say, cannot be used to correct a register drawn from the whole membership of a town's library. Ahlgren's reply concedes the imbalance but denies the conclusion. The claim, she writes, was never that commonplace books describe the general reader; it was that they reveal which passages, within a body of text already known to have circulated, readers found worth the labour of transcription — a question about texts rather than about populations, and one on which a skewed sample can still be informative provided its skew is stated.
accessibilityText: A two-paragraph passage about evidence for nineteenth-century reading habits. The first paragraph explains that historians have relied on library borrowing registers, which record each loan by title and borrower and are attractive because they can be counted, tabulated and compared across towns. It then objects that a register records a transaction rather than an encounter, since a book borrowed and returned unopened leaves the same trace as one read aloud nightly to a family of eight. It introduces a scholar named Ahlgren, who argues that the commonplace book, a personal notebook in which a reader copied passages that struck her, records the encounter, and that the two sources read together can distinguish what circulated from what was absorbed. The second paragraph gives the critics' objection, which concerns sampling: commonplace books survive in far smaller numbers than registers and survive unevenly, because the practice was taught in schools serving a narrow band of the population and because surviving notebooks come overwhelmingly from families prosperous enough to keep papers for a century, so critics say such a corpus cannot correct a register drawn from a whole town library's membership. Ahlgren replies by conceding the imbalance but denying the conclusion: she says her claim was never that commonplace books describe the general reader, but that they reveal which passages, within a body of text already known to have circulated, readers found worth transcribing, which is a question about texts rather than populations, and one on which a skewed sample can still be informative provided the skew is stated.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for the wave 3 top-up to support a new Reading Comprehension set. Book history and the study of commonplace books are real fields, but the scholar Ahlgren, the specific claims, the critics' objection and every sentence of the wording are invented for this item set and are not taken from, or paraphrased from, any ETS passage or any real publication.
